subject: embedded
title: Timing, Interrupts & Serial Buses
summary: Keep the main loop responsive, share work with an ISR safely, and trace UART, I2C and SPI transfers with explicit timing and protocol assumptions.

lessons.title: Choose polling or an interrupt
lessons.summary: Choose how to notice an event without hiding work or assuming every edge is retained.
lessons.body:
A button has changed or a serial byte has arrived. Firmware needs to notice, preserve any information that matters, and decide what work to perform. **Polling** and **interrupts** are two ways to arrange that work; neither automatically makes an application responsive.

## Check explicitly or handle an interrupt

With polling, the main loop repeatedly checks a status value. For example: check whether a receive buffer contains a byte, process a bounded amount of work, then check other devices. A blocking driver call can still prevent the next check, even if the rest of the loop looks simple.

With an interrupt, a configured hardware condition requests a processor exception. When the processor accepts it, execution enters an **interrupt service routine** (ISR), then later returns to interrupted work. An interrupt can be pending while another operation runs; masking, priority and current execution context affect when its handler executes. It is not an instantaneous callback.

An ISR should do the necessary bounded work: preserve data or record progress, acknowledge the source as the device requires, and defer longer processing to the main loop. Clearing a processor's pending bit and clearing the peripheral's underlying condition are not necessarily the same operation. Read that peripheral's procedure.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: checking a door or hearing a bell
> Someone can repeatedly look at the entrance or respond when a doorbell rings.
>
> **How it maps:** Looking is polling; the bell represents an interrupt request. A short response can record that someone arrived before the person returns to their main task.
>
> **Where it stops:** Hardware has precise masking, priority and acknowledgement rules. Several arrivals can produce one pending indication, and a bell does not guarantee that each arrival is counted.

## Trace the information you can lose

Suppose firmware checks a pin every 5 ms, at 0 ms, 5 ms and 10 ms. A pulse starts at 1 ms and ends at 2 ms. Every check sees the inactive level: polling the level misses that pulse.

An edge-capable peripheral may latch a request, but its behaviour must be configured and checked. A single pending flag can merge several events before service. A serial receive FIFO can retain several bytes but eventually fill. Choose the mechanism by the information required: latest state, a count of events, or every received byte.

Start with a cooperative loop when its measured check intervals meet the device's needs. Add an interrupt where hardware support and response requirements justify it. Measure the longest interval under realistic load, including driver calls and logging, rather than treating an average loop speed as a guarantee.

## Key takeaways
- Polling checks explicitly; an ISR runs when the processor accepts an interrupt request.
- Keep interrupt work bounded and acknowledge the actual device condition correctly.
- A pending indication need not preserve every event.

## Further reading
- [Arm CMSIS interrupt controller interfaces](https://arm-software.github.io/CMSIS_6/latest/Core/group__NVIC__gr.html)
- [Raspberry Pi SDK interrupt handling](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/master/src/rp2_common/hardware_irq/include/hardware/irq.h)

questions.prompt: A main loop reads a pin at 0 ms, 5 ms and 10 ms. A pulse is active from 1 ms until 2 ms. The hardware has no event latch. What will these reads show?

options.text: At least one active read.
options.explanation: The pulse ends before the next read at 5 ms, so no sample overlaps it.

options.text: Only the inactive level.
options.explanation: Correct. None of the three sampling times lies inside the active pulse.

options.text: Exactly two counted events.
options.explanation: Reading a level does not count the rising and falling edges, especially when both occur between reads.

options.text: A queued interrupt request.
options.explanation: The question specifies level reads and no event latch; software cannot assume an interrupt mechanism has preserved the pulse.

questions.workedExample:
1. The 0 ms read occurs earlier than the pulse.
2. The pulse ends at 2 ms, before the 5 ms read.
3. Both later reads also see inactive. A different observation or hardware capture mechanism is needed to retain this pulse.

questions.prompt: An interrupt-driven receiver sometimes overruns while its handler prints long diagnostic messages. Which changes address the problem? Select all that apply.

options.text: Preserve received data promptly and defer lengthy formatting.
options.explanation: Correct. Bounded handling reduces the time spent in the interrupt context; deferred processing still needs enough capacity.

options.text: Assume a pending flag counts every incoming byte.
options.explanation: A pending indication can merge events; it is not a substitute for retaining the received data.

options.text: Check FIFO capacity, overflow reporting and the rate at which data is drained.
options.explanation: Correct. An interrupt does not remove finite buffering or limits on sustained processing throughput.

options.text: Acknowledge the peripheral using its documented procedure.
options.explanation: Correct. Handling the underlying source correctly prevents leaving the condition asserted or clearing the wrong information.

questions.workedExample:
1. Long logging delays other useful work. Move lengthy processing out of the handler.
2. Retain the actual bytes and inspect hardware/driver overflow indicators.
3. Follow the device acknowledgement procedure; a processor pending bit alone may not clear the device condition.

questions.prompt: A peripheral has one pending flag. Three events occur before firmware services it, and the device retains no count or FIFO. What can a true flag establish?

options.text: Exactly three events occurred.
options.explanation: The single flag cannot distinguish one event from several events merged into the pending state.

options.text: No data can have been lost.
options.explanation: The flag provides no capacity guarantee for information it never stored.

options.text: At least one relevant event became pending, but the exact count is unknown.
options.explanation: Correct. Several event histories can lead to the same single pending indication.

options.text: The handler began at the instant of the first event.
options.explanation: A pending request can wait because of masking, priorities or current execution context.

questions.workedExample:
1. One event can set the flag.
2. Later events can leave the same flag set without adding distinguishable state.
3. Therefore the true flag does not recover the exact event count.

lessons.title: Measure elapsed time without blocking
lessons.summary: Use unsigned elapsed-time subtraction with an explicit counter width and observation bound.

questions.prompt: A millisecond counter uses `uint32_t`. A saved start is `UINT32_MAX - 3u`; the current reading is `6u`. Actual elapsed time is known to be less than one complete counter cycle. Does `(uint32_t)(now - start) >= 10u` report the timer due?

options.text: No, because the current reading is numerically smaller.
options.explanation: That compares display positions instead of using unsigned elapsed-time subtraction.

options.text: It has undefined signed-overflow behaviour on every C implementation.
options.explanation: The explicit conversion to the exact unsigned width gives modulo behaviour; the example is not a signed-overflow timer design.

options.text: No, because the difference must be six.
options.explanation: Six counts have passed since zero, but four more counts take the old reading to zero.

options.text: Yes: the unsigned elapsed value is ten.
options.explanation: Correct. Four increments reach zero and six more reach six, within the stated observation bound.

questions.workedExample:
1. From UINT32_MAX minus three, four increments reach zero.
2. Six further increments reach the current count six.
3. The elapsed count is ten, so the comparison with ten is true. The known less-than-one-cycle bound is essential.

link.title: C11 draft: unsigned arithmetic and conversions

questions.prompt: Firmware saves a 32-bit tick reading and then stops checking for more than a whole counter cycle. The next unsigned difference is small. What can firmware conclude from that difference alone?

options.text: Only the elapsed remainder; the number of complete missed cycles is unknown.
options.explanation: Correct. Different actual durations can have the same modulo-width difference.

options.text: The actual pause was definitely short.
options.explanation: A complete cycle can return the display to the same position.

options.text: Changing the comparison to signed integers reconstructs missed cycles.
options.explanation: Changing interpretation does not recover information the counter did not retain.

options.text: The hardware timer stopped during the pause.
options.explanation: A small wrapped difference does not establish anything about timer stoppage.

questions.workedExample:
1. The counter stores a position in a finite repeating range.
2. Adding one complete range leaves the same position.
3. Without another time source or an observation bound, the actual number of missed cycles is not recoverable.

link.title: C11 draft: unsigned arithmetic and conversions

questions.prompt: A task uses a non-blocking timer with a 10 ms interval. It was due at 50 ms but the loop handles it at 55 ms, then saves 55 ms as its new start. Assuming timely future checks, when is it next due under that policy?

options.text: 60 ms, because all timer policies preserve the original phase.
options.explanation: Saving the actual handling time restarts this policy from 55 ms.

options.text: 65 ms.
options.explanation: Correct. The next interval begins at the newly saved start, so the late check shifts the schedule.

options.text: Immediately and repeatedly until every missed instant is replayed.
options.explanation: That is a catch-up policy, not the stated restart-from-now policy.

options.text: Exactly 55 ms, because elapsed time is always due after rollover.
options.explanation: Immediately after saving the new start the elapsed count is zero.

questions.workedExample:
1. The task chooses a new starting marker of 55 ms.
2. Another 10 ms interval ends at 65 ms.
3. An alternative fixed-period schedule could preserve phase, but would need its own late-work policy.

lessons.title: Share events with an interrupt safely
lessons.summary: Protect a read-and-clear operation under explicit single-core interrupt assumptions.

questions.prompt: A shared event count contains three. Foreground code copies three locally; an ISR increments the shared count to four; foreground code then clears the shared count to zero and processes its local three. What happened?

options.text: The fourth event was preserved by volatile.
options.explanation: Volatile access does not combine the foreground copy and clear into one indivisible operation.

options.text: Four events will be processed from the local copy.
options.explanation: The local copy was taken before the interrupt incremented the shared count.

options.text: One event was lost from the software accounting.
options.explanation: Correct. The interrupt increment was overwritten by the later clear, while the local copy still held three.

options.text: This sequence proves there are two CPU cores.
options.explanation: The ISR can interrupt foreground code on the same core between the copy and clear.

questions.workedExample:
1. The local copy retains three.
2. The ISR records a fourth event in the shared value.
3. The later foreground clear overwrites that new value, so the copied work accounts for only three events.

questions.prompt: A Pico SDK function calls `save_and_disable_interrupts()` before a short shared-state operation. The caller had already disabled interrupts. What should the function do on exit?

options.text: Unconditionally enable interrupts.
options.explanation: That would change the caller's execution state and may expose a surrounding protected operation.

options.text: Leave all interrupts disabled forever.
options.explanation: The function should restore the saved state; another caller might have entered with interrupts enabled.

options.text: Clear every peripheral pending flag.
options.explanation: Interrupt state restoration is not permission to discard unrelated device events.

options.text: Pass the saved state to the matching restore helper.
options.explanation: Correct. Restoring the prior state preserves whether the caller entered with interrupts enabled or disabled.

questions.workedExample:
1. The save helper returns the previous interrupt state on the calling core.
2. The protected operation must remain short.
3. Restoring that saved state preserves an already-disabled caller instead of accidentally enabling interrupts.

questions.prompt: A design shares work between foreground code and an ISR. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A true/false flag can merge multiple arrivals into one indication.
options.explanation: Correct. Repeatedly setting an already-true flag does not add an event count.

options.text: Disabling interrupts on one core also stops the other core from accessing the data.
options.explanation: The SDK helper affects the calling core; it is not a multicore lock.

options.text: A shared counter still needs an overflow policy or a justified no-overflow bound.
options.explanation: Correct. Its finite range cannot retain an unlimited number of events.

options.text: An atomic type must be checked for suitability on the actual target before using it in an ISR.
options.explanation: Correct. The operation must meet the target/compiler/SDK requirements; not every atomic implementation is appropriate for interrupt context.

questions.workedExample:
1. Decide whether the application needs latest state, event counts or ordered data.
2. Exclude the actual competing actors; a calling-core interrupt mask does not exclude another core.
3. Check storage capacity and whether the chosen primitive is suitable for the real interrupt environment.

lessons.title: Read a UART frame and budget its bytes
lessons.summary: Separate UART framing, payload rate and the receive buffer that software must drain.
lessons.body:
A **UART**, or universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter, converts bytes into a serial bit stream and reconstructs received bytes. A common full-duplex connection uses a transmit signal in each direction, plus the electrical reference required by the interface. Asynchronous means there is no separate shared bit-clock wire; each end uses its configured timing.

Both ends must agree on baud rate, data bits, parity and stop bits. Pin functions and electrical levels are separate requirements. Work only with low-voltage development hardware. Use a board-approved adapter and the device manuals: a UART framing setting does not establish a safe voltage, and an RS-232 electrical interface is not directly interchangeable with a microcontroller's logic-level pins.

## Count framing as well as payload

Assume an ordinary binary UART link with **8N1** framing: one start bit, eight data bits, no parity and one stop bit. That is ten transmitted bit periods for one payload byte, before any gaps between frames.

```formula
T = N × b / R
T = (96 × 10 / 9600) s
T = 0.1 s = 100 ms
where
T: ideal wire time for the data, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
N: number of payload bytes, here 96
b: transmitted bits per byte under the assumed framing, here 10 for 8N1
R: line rate in bits per second, here 9600; for this binary UART signalling it matches 9600 baud
s: second
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
In words: 96 payload bytes need 960 line bits, taking 100 milliseconds at 9600 bits per second, before any additional gaps.
```

A UART's FIFO and any software receive buffer provide temporary storage. They do not increase the sustained drain rate. If input keeps arriving faster than software consumes it, a finite buffer eventually overflows. An overrun can lose data; check the hardware and driver error reporting.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: letters arriving in a tray
> A tray can hold letters while someone is busy, but it eventually fills if letters arrive faster than they are opened.
>
> **How it maps:** UART receive buffers hold a bounded amount of incoming data until firmware reads it. A larger buffer buys time during a pause, not unlimited sustained capacity.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real UARTs have framing and error flags, and their buffers retain bytes rather than whole application messages. A tray does not define when one command ends.

## Give the byte stream a meaning

For a first text command protocol, agree a terminator such as a newline and a maximum command length. Accumulate bytes until the terminator, reject an overlong command, and decide how to resynchronise. For binary messages, use a specified length and framing scheme. Receiving one byte is not the same as receiving a complete valid command.

Trace `O`, `N`, newline: the parser stores the first two bytes and handles the command only when the terminator arrives. A receive call may return before, at or after those three bytes have arrived; preserve the parser's partial state across calls. Keep interrupt receive work short and perform command interpretation outside the ISR where possible.

## Key takeaways
- UART timing and framing must agree at both ends; electrical compatibility is separate.
- Include start, data, parity and stop bits when estimating wire time.
- Buffers are finite, and application messages need their own framing rules.

## Further reading
- [TI: RS-232 electrical interface and logic-level conversion](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slla607/slla607.pdf)
- [Pico SDK UART framing and receive interfaces](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/master/src/rp2_common/hardware_uart/include/hardware/uart.h)
- [RP2040 datasheet: UART peripheral](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2040/rp2040-datasheet.pdf)

questions.prompt: A binary UART sends 96 payload bytes at 9600 baud using one start bit, eight data bits, no parity and one stop bit per byte. There are no extra gaps. What is the ideal wire time?

options.explanation: Correct. There are ten line bits per payload byte, so 960 bits take one tenth of a second.

options.text: 80 ms.
options.explanation: That counts only eight payload bits and omits start and stop bits.

options.text: 10 ms.
options.explanation: The whole message contains 960 line bits, not 96 line bits.

options.text: Exactly 100 ms in every real application.
options.explanation: The calculated value is the ideal no-gap wire time, not a guarantee including driver waits or application delays.

questions.workedExample:
```formula
T = N × b / R
T = (96 × 10 / 9600) s
T = 0.1 s = 100 ms
where
T: ideal transfer time in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
N: payload bytes, here 96
b: line bits per payload byte, here 10 for the stated start/data/stop format
R: binary line rate, here 9600 bits per second, matching 9600 baud in this example
s: second
ms: millisecond, one thousandth of a second
In words: 96 framed bytes take 100 milliseconds before any extra gaps or software delays.
```

questions.prompt: Which checks belong in a robust beginner UART receiver? Select all that apply.

options.text: Specify a maximum application command length and what ends a command.
options.explanation: Correct. UART byte framing does not define the application's message boundaries or allowed length.

options.text: Check overrun or receive-error reporting and drain buffers fast enough.
options.explanation: Correct. Hardware and software buffering are finite.

options.text: Treat matching baud rates as proof of safe electrical compatibility.
options.explanation: Baud rate is a timing setting, not a voltage or wiring compatibility guarantee.

options.text: Keep partial parsing state when a command arrives over several reads.
options.explanation: Correct. A receive function need not return exactly one whole application command.

questions.workedExample:
1. Configure matching serial timing and verify electrical compatibility separately.
2. Retain bounded partial command state across receives.
3. Detect errors and overlong messages, and define a recovery path instead of relying on unlimited buffering.

questions.prompt: A text protocol defines newline as its command terminator. So far the receiver has read only `O` and `N`. What should it normally do?

options.text: Execute ON immediately because two bytes always make a UART frame.
options.explanation: A UART frame here carries one byte; it does not define a two-byte application command.

options.text: Keep the partial command until newline arrives or a specified error/limit is reached.
options.explanation: Correct. The application framing rule says the command is not complete yet.

options.text: Discard both bytes because every receive call must contain a whole command.
options.explanation: Read boundaries do not have to match application message boundaries.

options.text: Wait forever inside the interrupt handler for the newline.
options.explanation: Unbounded waiting in the ISR can prevent other work and worsen receive problems.

questions.workedExample:
1. The UART has delivered bytes, not a complete command.
2. Store the bounded partial state for O and N.
3. Complete the command only when the agreed terminator arrives, subject to the protocol's limits and failure policy.

lessons.title: Trace an I2C register read
lessons.summary: Distinguish a seven-bit target address, wire address byte and the final read NACK.
lessons.body:
Ordinary bidirectional **I2C** uses two shared signals: **SDA** for data and **SCL** for the clock. Devices pull a signal low or release it; pull-up resistors bring released lines high. Work only with low-voltage development hardware. Check the board, target-device and bus specifications for suitable levels and pull-ups rather than assuming a universal resistor value.

A controller initiates a transfer and addresses a target. We use a single-controller bus with seven-bit addressing in this lesson. Device-specific commands and register layouts still come from the target's datasheet: “uses I2C” does not specify how to read its measurements.

## A fictional one-byte sensor register

Assume a fictional target has seven-bit address `0x48`, selects a register by a one-byte write, and returns that register on a following read with a repeated START. Its register `0x01` currently contains `0x7A`. This is a protocol exercise, not a claim about an actual sensor.

| Step | Sender | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| START | Controller | Begin transfer |
| `0x90` | Controller | Address `0x48`, write direction |
| ACK | Target | Accept address |
| `0x01` | Controller | Select the fictional register |
| ACK | Target | Accept register byte |
| Repeated START | Controller | Begin another address phase |
| `0x91` | Controller | Address `0x48`, read direction |
| ACK | Target | Accept address |
| `0x7A` | Target | Return the fictional register byte |
| NACK, then STOP | Controller | Finish this one-byte read |

The first wire byte combines the seven address bits and the read/write bit. The Pico SDK's I2C API accepts the seven-bit address separately; it supplies the direction bit. Passing `0x90` where that API expects `0x48` confuses two different representations.

**ACK** means the receiving side acknowledged that byte. It is not proof that a measurement is fresh or meaningful. A **NACK** at the end of the controller's last read byte is the normal way to decline another byte, whereas an address NACK can indicate that the selected target did not respond.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: addressing a letter and asking for a reply
> A sender identifies the recipient, delivers a request and then allows the recipient to reply before ending the exchange.
>
> **How it maps:** The address selects a target; the write selects the fictional register; the repeated START changes the transfer direction without ending that combined exchange.
>
> **Where it stops:** I2C has precise clocked byte and acknowledgement rules, and a target's command sequence is device-specific. An acknowledged address does not identify which of two incorrectly duplicated-address devices replied.

## Stop failures becoming a frozen loop

Use a driver operation with a suitable timeout and check its result and returned byte count. Devices may stretch the clock in modes that allow it; a broken connection or stuck signal also needs a bounded failure path. A timeout is a software decision to stop waiting, not proof that the underlying wiring has recovered. Retry only under a deliberate policy; report the fault if recovery fails.

## Key takeaways
- Distinguish a seven-bit API address from the address-and-direction byte on the wire.
- Read the target's command protocol; there is no universal sensor register map.
- Interpret NACK in context and bound failed transfers.

## Further reading
- [NXP UM10204: I2C protocol and acknowledgement](https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/user-guide/UM10204.pdf)
- [Pico SDK I2C addressing and timeout APIs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/master/src/rp2_common/hardware_i2c/include/hardware/i2c.h)

questions.prompt: An I2C device has seven-bit address `0x48`. Its write-direction address byte on the wire is `0x90`. The Pico SDK call expects a seven-bit address parameter. Which value belongs in that parameter?

options.explanation: That is the already-combined wire address byte; this API supplies the direction bit itself.
That is the read-direction wire byte, not the seven-bit API address.
Correct. Pass the target's seven-bit address to this API, which adds the direction bit.

options.text: The register number instead of the target address.
options.explanation: The target address selects the device; register selection belongs to the device-specific data sequence.

questions.workedExample:
1. Separate the target address from the direction of this transfer.
2. The seven-bit target address remains 0x48.
3. The documented SDK API constructs the wire address phase, so an already-shifted address is incorrect.

questions.prompt: A controller reads exactly one byte from an I2C target, then sends NACK followed by STOP. The target acknowledged its address and supplied the byte. What does that final NACK mean here?

options.text: The target's address was necessarily wrong.
options.explanation: An address NACK would occur in the address acknowledgement position, not as the controller's final response to received data.

options.text: Every read must continue forever until the target sends NACK.
options.explanation: The controller-receiver decides when it has received the requested data and ends the read using the specified protocol.

options.text: The byte is guaranteed fresh sensor data.
options.explanation: Protocol acknowledgement behaviour does not establish the meaning or freshness of a measurement.

options.text: The controller is declining another byte and ending this read normally.
options.explanation: Correct. NACK after the final controller-received byte is normal termination for this read.

questions.workedExample:
1. The target already acknowledged its address.
2. The controller received its requested byte.
3. The controller then indicates that it wants no more bytes and issues STOP; this is not an address-failure indication.

questions.prompt: A beginner I2C measurement loop must remain responsive when a target is disconnected. Which choices are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use an operation with a suitable timeout and check its result and byte count.
options.explanation: Correct. A failed exchange needs a bounded software path and an explicit outcome.

options.text: Assume any ACK proves the returned measurement is fresh.
options.explanation: Acknowledging a byte does not prove that its application-level contents are fresh or valid.

options.text: Treat timeout as a fault to report or handle under a deliberate recovery policy.
options.explanation: Correct. Stopping the wait does not itself repair the electrical bus or target.

options.text: Retry forever inside the main loop without checking other work.
options.explanation: Unbounded retrying can freeze the rest of the cooperative application.

questions.workedExample:
1. A disconnected target may fail to acknowledge; other faults can also prevent progress.
2. A timeout limits the waiting operation, after which firmware must inspect the result.
3. Recovery is a separate policy, and persistent failure should become a visible fault rather than an infinite retry loop.

lessons.title: Match SPI clocks and chip selection
lessons.summary: Use a peripheral datasheet to set SPI sampling edges, selection and exchange boundaries.
lessons.body:
A common four-signal **SPI**, or serial peripheral interface, connects a controller and a peripheral with a clock, data in each direction and **chip select**. The controller supplies clock pulses. The two data directions can shift bits during the same clocks, although a particular command may use only one direction's useful result.

Signal names vary. A controller's data output is often called COPI or MOSI; its data input is CIPO or MISO. Follow the actual device labels and directions, not just familiar wire colours. Work only with low-voltage development hardware. Check electrical compatibility and the board's pin-function configuration before connecting devices.

## Agree which edge means sample

**Clock polarity** (CPOL) chooses the idle clock level. **Clock phase** (CPHA) chooses which clock edge samples a bit relative to that idle level. In the commonly named mode 0, the clock idles low and the receiver samples on the leading, rising edge; subsequent data changes happen on trailing, falling edges. The first transmitted bit must already be valid before the first sampling edge.

Do not memorise “always read on rising edges”: a different required mode can use different edges. Configure the mode, bit order, number of bits per transfer and maximum clock rate specified by the peripheral. Also respect chip select setup and hold times; lowering the clock rate does not fix the wrong sampling mode.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a leader setting the beat
> Two people pass items in time with a leader's beat. They must agree which part of the beat means present an item and which means take it.
>
> **How it maps:** The controller's clock sets the transfer rhythm, and the configured sampling edge determines when a bit must be valid. Chip select identifies the intended exchange.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real devices specify exact timing, bit order and chip select behaviour. Matching a beat does not establish a shared command language or prove that the receiver accepted a command.

## Trace a command without inventing a device

Assume a fictional peripheral uses an active-low chip select and requires a command byte followed by one dummy byte, all within one selection. It returns status while the dummy byte is clocked. This is that fictional device's rule, not a universal SPI frame format.

1. Drive its chip select active using the required timing.
2. Transfer the command byte and discard the simultaneously received placeholder.
3. Transfer the dummy byte while collecting the returned status.
4. Wait for the transfer to finish, then deassert chip select at the allowed time.

A transmit function returning can mean data entered a buffer rather than that the last clock finished; use the documented driver semantics. The Pico SDK's blocking transfer operations are one concrete example to inspect, rather than assuming every API means the same thing.

SPI itself does not provide I2C-style addressing and per-byte ACK. Check the returned device status or other documented evidence. For multiple peripherals sharing a data-return wire, each unselected device must release it as its datasheet requires; chip-select wiring alone does not prove the bus is electrically shareable.

## Key takeaways
- Match polarity, phase, bits per transfer, bit order and rate to the device's specification.
- Chip select timing and command framing belong to the peripheral's protocol.
- Clocking bits does not itself prove successful application-level communication.

## Further reading
- [Pico SDK SPI format and transfer semantics](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/master/src/rp2_common/hardware_spi/include/hardware/spi.h)
- [RP2040 datasheet: SPI peripheral timing](https://datasheets.raspberrypi.com/rp2040/rp2040-datasheet.pdf)

questions.prompt: A peripheral requires SPI mode 0. Under the conventional CPOL/CPHA naming used here, what does the receiver do?

options.text: Idle the clock low and sample on each leading rising edge.
options.explanation: Correct. Mode 0 uses CPOL zero and CPHA zero; data must be valid before the sampling edge.

options.text: Sample only when chip select changes.
options.explanation: Chip select marks the exchange; the clock's configured edges sample the bits.

options.text: Idle the clock high and always sample falling edges.
options.explanation: That describes a different mode convention, not the stated mode 0 configuration.

options.text: Choose any mode as long as the clock is slow.
options.explanation: A slower rate does not change which edge the peripheral expects for sampling.

questions.workedExample:
1. CPOL zero makes the idle clock low.
2. CPHA zero selects the leading edge for sampling.
3. The leading edge from a low idle level is rising; the first data bit must already be valid.

questions.prompt: A fictional SPI device requires a command byte and then a dummy byte during one active-low chip select interval. The status arrives during the dummy byte. What is the correct exchange outline?

options.text: Send the command, deassert chip select, then read the old command byte as status.
options.explanation: That breaks the fictional device's stated exchange boundary and reads the wrong part of the exchange.

options.text: Drive chip select active, send command, clock a dummy byte while receiving status, wait for completion, then release selection.
options.explanation: Correct. It follows the stated device-specific frame and preserves the selection through both transfers.

options.text: Wait for the peripheral to generate its own SPI clock.
options.explanation: The controller supplies clocks in the controller-led interface described here.

options.text: Send only the command because SPI always queues a later status packet.
options.explanation: SPI supplies no universal response packet framing; this device explicitly returns status during the dummy transfer.

questions.workedExample:
1. Select this device with its specified timing.
2. Transfer the command and then the dummy byte without ending the selection.
3. Collect the second received byte as status, wait for the final transfer to finish, and release selection as required.

questions.prompt: A controller clocks an SPI exchange and its transfer call completes. Which statements remain correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: SPI provides an I2C-style ACK after every byte, so success is proven.
options.explanation: The usual SPI transfer does not have that per-byte I2C acknowledgement mechanism.

options.text: The device's documented returned status may still need validation.
options.explanation: Correct. Successful clocking does not establish that the peripheral understood or accepted the command.

options.text: Chip select timing and the device's command framing still matter.
options.explanation: Correct. SPI electrical transfer settings do not define the peripheral's full command protocol.

options.text: Every unselected device is guaranteed to release a shared return wire regardless of its datasheet.
options.explanation: Electrical sharing requirements must be checked for the actual devices; selection wiring alone is insufficient.

questions.workedExample:
1. A completed transfer establishes only the documented driver-level outcome.
2. The peripheral protocol determines where status appears and what it means.
3. Validate that outcome and meet the peripheral's selection and timing requirements.
